rv.q: But, believe me, meta isn’t better. Myrtle fights with the director (Hadley Fraser), plays opposite her ex-lover (Benjamin Walker), belittles the playwright (Nicola Hughes, excellent) and is mooned over by the producer (John Marquez).
It may be the most unusual thing on the London stage right now and is captivating in its glittering strangeness.
...it’s not really a musical at all, but rather a play that uses songs to specific effect.

Thank God also for Rufus Wainwright's music. True, it sometimes dwindles into semi-tonal burbling. But it also explodes with the singer-songwriter's gift for doomed glory. A spectacular duet with Nicola Hughes as an exasperated writer character even brought to mind the brassy swagger of All That Jaz...
Now recognised as an audacious masterpiece, it was the inspiration for The Second Woman — the 24-hour-epic delivered by Ruth Wilson last year — and it drives this similarl...
...this new musical displays a maddening lack of focus.
Sheridan Smith enthralls, but this play is a pretentious, convoluted mess

And when you do work out what’s going on — clue: it’s usually Smith’s star-actress character Myrtle losing the plot once again as she struggles to get her head right for her soon-to-open Broadway play — you’re hard pushed to care. Still, let’s pause to salute Smith because there won’t be a lot of saluting to follow.
This take on John Cassavetes’ 1977 film is unsalvageable

The script tries – but fails – to make us believe that Myrtle is haunted by the young woman’s spirit, while poor Haas is left to prance provocatively but pointlessly around in a short skirt and stockings.

Smith’s fans may be startled by her taking on such a tale. After all, she suffered mental health struggles herself during her run of Funny Girl in 2016 and missed a series of performances. But, as Smith has explained in interviews, Opening Night is a deliberate choice to confront those demons: tackling life via theatre.

But it is a musical, and one where everyone is angry, characters shout at each other constantly and it very quickly becomes irritating. Sarah Goode, played by Nicola Hughes is in a permanent state of bad temper, so much so, that by the act one finale the character comes across more like an embittere...
...it is one of the most baffling wastes of talent.

The result is that you end up watching Smith singing more often than not through tears whilst inhabiting an actress called Myrtle Gordon (great name!) in throes to a breakdown as the Broadway play in which she is starring crawls towards opening night. Release, one senses, awaits both on the character's behalf – and our own.

At the start of the second half of Ivo Van Hove’s production of his own musical version of John Cassavetes‘ ultra-Seventies backstager “Opening Night” — with music and lyrics by Rufus Wainwright — the words “the aftermath” (in fashionable lower case) appear on the large screen that dominates the sta...
I've rarely seen a production more determined to confuse and frustrate an audience.

In a London auditorium, a work of art is being desecrated. “Opening Night,” John Cassavetes’s understatedly stylish 1977 movie about an actress struggling with midlife ennui, has been reimagined as a musical by the Belgian director Ivo van Hove, and the result is a travesty.
How exciting in theory, then, to have a new musical by Rufus Wainwright, with his dual talent of big tunes and lyrics often so poignantly mundane.

Been there, seen that in Jamie Lloyd’s Sunset Boulevard. Smith holds the centre with her customary flair but she and the entire cast are visibly struggling with Wainwright’s banal lyrics (“You’ve got to make magic/Magic out of tragic”) and blandly conventional music as well as Van Hove’s dialogue that consists of showbiz cliches strung together ...
The production is more like a multi-lane pile-up, complete with overturned leaking oil tanker, giant sinkholes and possibly an earthquake, asteroid or charging rhino or two.

cn.t: Critics savage this Cassavetes adaptation as an unfocused, convoluted mess that wastes its talent, though Sheridan Smith's raw performance and Rufus Wainwright's music earn scattered praise amid the wreckage.
